structure.rationale: The book follows the split the requester specified: Part 1 (The Plan 9 Model) lays down the three composing pillars — files as the uniform resource interface, 9P as the single protocol that reaches them, and the per-process namespace that assembles them into a program's view — using the 'Plan 9 from Bell Labs' overview paper as the grounding source, with no history or biography. Part 2 then walks outward from the same three pillars in dependency order: Namespaces (the abstraction itself) before 9P Protocol (the wire mechanism namespaces are built from) before File Servers (the things namespaces name and 9P talks to); Mount, Bind, and Union Directories follow as the operators that construct a namespace from those servers; Process Namespaces then shows how that construction interacts with rfork/process lifecycle; Plumbing is placed next as a worked example of the whole model — an ordinary file server used as an interprocess bus; and Security and the Capability Model closes the book, since Plan 9's security design (no setuid, factotum, capabilities) is best understood as a consequence of everything established before it — namespace restriction standing in for privilege. Each concept builds strictly on the ones before it, so a reader who proceeds in order never meets an unexplained mechanism.
structure.audience: Technically savvy readers already comfortable with systems programming and Unix-family OS concepts, who want Plan 9's actual design and mechanisms — not its history — explained precisely.
